sections.body:
Clothes are the things we wear on our body. We wear them for three reasons.

First, we wear clothes to be comfortable. A soft shirt feels nice on your skin. Loose clothes let you move and run and jump.

Second, we wear clothes for the weather. In Vietnam the weather changes in a day. It can be hot and sunny at noon, then cool and rainy in the afternoon. Clothes help our body keep the right temperature.

Third, we wear clothes for special days. A school uniform tells people you are a pupil. A áo dài is worn at a festival or a family celebration. A football shirt shows which team you support.

Clothes come in many shapes and colours. Some are close fitting. Some are loose. Some have short sleeves. Some have long sleeves and cover your hands.

What you wear says something about you. It shows your mood, your family, and the kind of day you are having. That is why choosing clothes is a real skill, and why grown-ups help you learn it.
examples: These are my clothes for school.
I wear a jacket because the rain is coming.
This shirt is too small for me now.
sections.heading: What clothes are, and why we wear them

sections.body:
Let us go from the top of the body downwards.

On your head you wear a **hat**, a **cap** or a **helmet**. A helmet protects your head when you ride a bike or a motorbike.

On your body you wear a **shirt** or a **T-shirt**. In the south of Vietnam a shirt with buttons is an **áo sơ mi**. A **jumper** is a warm knitted top you wear in the cool weather.

On your legs you wear **trousers** or **shorts**. In Vietnam we also say **quần**. A **skirt** is worn by many girls and women. **Jeans** are strong trousers made of denim.

On your feet you wear **socks** and **shoes**. **Trainers** are soft shoes for sport. **Sandals** are shoes with open sides, good for hot days.

There are clothes for special jobs too. An **apron** protects your clothes while you cook. **Gloves** keep your hands warm or clean. **Socks and shoes** are the parts that get dirty first, so they are the parts you change most often.
examples: I wear a cap when the sun is strong.
These trousers are too long, so I roll them up.
sections.heading: The clothes we wear every day

sections.body:
The weather changes, and your clothes should change with it.

On a **hot day**, wear light, loose clothes in a pale colour. White and light colours reflect the sun. A hat and a bottle of water protect you from the sun.

On a **cold day**, wear layers. A **layer** is one thin piece of clothing over another. A vest over a shirt, and a jacket over that, keeps you warm, and you can take one off when it gets hot.

On a **rainy day**, wear a **raincoat** or a **jacket** with a water-repellent surface. Water-repellent means the water runs off instead of soaking in. Rubber boots keep your feet dry. An **umbrella** keeps the rain off your head and your school bag.

In Vietnam the wind blows colder in the months we call the dry season, so a windbreaker jacket is useful then.

Check the weather before you leave the house. Say what the day will be like out loud: hot, cool, windy or wet. Then choose. That way you will not be cold on the bus, or too hot in the classroom.
examples: It is very hot, so I wear a loose white shirt.
It is cold today, so I wear a jacket over my shirt.
I take an umbrella because it is going to rain.
sections.heading: Choosing clothes for the weather

sections.body:
These are the words for the clothes you wear. Learn them and you can shop for yourself.

A **shirt** is a top with a collar that you wear over your body.

Trousers are the two pieces of cloth you wear on your legs, one for each leg.

Socks are the soft cloth you wear on your feet inside your shoes.

Shoes cover your feet. Every pair has a left shoe and a right shoe, and they do not match if you put them on the wrong way round.

A **jacket** is a thicker top you wear over your shirt when it is cold or wet.

One easy way to remember these words is to touch each thing as you say it. Shirt, trousers, socks, shoes, jacket. Do it in the morning and by lunch you will know them.
examples: I need a jacket because of the rain.
sections.heading: The clothes words, one by one

terms.example: My school shirt has a blue collar.
terms.gloss: A top with a collar that you wear over your body, on its own or under a jacket.

terms.example: I put on my trousers before my socks.
terms.gloss: Clothes you wear on your legs, one piece for each leg.

terms.example: These socks are too big for me.
terms.gloss: Soft cloth you wear on your feet, inside your shoes.

terms.example: I put on my shoes by the door.
terms.gloss: Hard things you wear on your feet. One is for the left foot and one for the right.

terms.example: I wear a jacket when it is cold in the morning.
terms.gloss: A thicker top you wear over your shirt when it is cold or wet.

sections.body:
Getting dressed is easier when you keep to the same order. Try this one and it will become automatic.

Start with the clothes. Lay everything out on the bed first. Check that it is all there.

Then put on your **underwear**, and your **socks** next. Socks go on before shoes, and trousers go over socks.

Next, put on your **trousers**. If they are too long, roll them up once.

Then your **shirt**. Pull it down so it sits properly, and tuck it in if you are wearing a belt.

Now the outer things. Put on your **jacket** or **sweater**, and your **shoes**.

Last, check yourself. Is everything straight? Are the shoes on the right feet? Are your hands cold? Then you are ready.
examples: I lay my clothes out on the bed first.
I check my shoes before I leave.
sections.heading: How to get dressed by yourself
steps: Lay all your clothes out on the bed and check them.
Put on your underwear and your socks.
Pull on your trousers and roll them up if they are too long.
Put on your shirt and make it sit straight.
Put on your jacket or sweater and your shoes.
Check that everything is straight before you go.

sections.body:
Clothes last longer when you look after them. A few small habits do a lot.

Take off your outdoor shoes at the door. Indoors we wear slippers or bare feet, and the floor stays clean.

If you spill something on your clothes, do not rub it. Blot it gently with a clean cloth, then tell an adult. Rubbing pushes the mark deeper into the cloth.

Wash your clothes at the right temperature. Very hot water can shrink a shirt. The label on the inside of the shirt tells you what to do.

Fold your clothes instead of throwing them on the chair. Hang the shirts on hangers, so they keep their shape. A hanger keeps a shirt looking neat.

And if a piece of clothing is too small, do not keep wearing it hoping it will grow. Ask for a bigger size, and give the old one away to a smaller child.
examples: I take my shoes off at the door.
I blot the mark instead of rubbing it.
My shirt is too small, so mother buys me a bigger one.
sections.heading: Taking care of your clothes

item.summary: Clothes keep you comfortable, warm or cool, and ready for the day. After reading this, you can name the clothes you wear, choose the right one for the weather, and get dressed on your own.
item.title: Clothes We Wear Every Day
